brief.situation: Handover at 18:00 in the surgical ICU. Bed 4, 66-year-old man, 80 kg, open pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple) for a pancreatic head mass, finished at 13:00. Extubated in the OR. Arterial line, central line, urinary catheter, NG tube, two abdominal drains (left drain beside the pancreatic anastomosis). Hydromorphone PCA.
handover: HR 84, ABP 128/72 (MAP 91), CVP 8, SpO2 98% on 2 L, RR 14, urine 60 mL/h, temperature 36.4 C.
Drains: thin pink fluid, about 30 mL/h together. Dressing dry.
Post-op Hgb 11.2 g/dL at 15:00, lactate 1.4, ionized calcium 1.15. Type and screen from this morning.
Standing order: lactated Ringer's boluses up to 1 L for MAP under 65 or urine under 0.5 mL/kg/h, then call the surgeon. Blood products and vasoactive drugs need the surgeon's order.
howItWorks: The clock runs in real time at the pace you choose: study pace (3x) or exam realism (1x). Pause any time.
Assessments examine him; orders act. Some ask for a volume or a dose.
Everything takes as long as it would on a real unit: boluses and units run in over minutes, the surgeon calls back and walks over, blood and labs take time.
While you wait on something, Skip jumps ahead, says how much time it skips and logs it. The bleeding keeps going at the same rate.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. Then a debrief scores what you did.

whatIsHappening.question: He has changed since handover. What do you think is happening, and what will you do first?

parts.label: What is happening
parts.criteria: Names post-operative hemorrhage (bleeding into the abdomen) with early hemorrhagic shock and supports it with at least two of: rising heart rate, narrowing pulse pressure, bright red drain output, a firmer or more distended abdomen, falling urine output, cool skin or restlessness, rising lactate. Recognizes that a near-normal blood pressure or first hemoglobin does not rule it out.
parts.modelAnswer: Post-operative bleeding into the abdomen with compensated hemorrhagic shock: HR up 20 or more since handover, pulse pressure narrowing, the left drain turning bright red, a firmer abdomen, restlessness and cooler hands. The blood pressure is held up by compensation and the first hemoglobin lags behind acute blood loss, so neither rules it out.

parts.label: What first
parts.criteria: Calls the surgeon to the bedside now (an early bleed from the operative bed needs a return to the OR); gives blood early (emergency-release units, massive transfusion protocol) rather than more crystalloid; mentions at least one of warming, calcium, or labs including type and crossmatch; does not plan to chase a normal pressure with fluid or a vasopressor.
parts.modelAnswer: Page the surgeon with an SBAR asking them to come now, because the fix is surgical. Get emergency-release blood and activate the massive transfusion protocol, give plasma with the red cells, keep crystalloid to a short bridge, warm him, check ionized calcium and replace it, and send labs with a type and crossmatch. Agree a pressure target with the surgeon rather than chasing a normal one.

Leaves for the OR within 45 min of the bleed starting (expert path about 33 min).

arrest.label: Cardiac arrest from blood loss
arrest.narrative: The monitor shows a narrow-complex rhythm, but there is no pulse on the arterial line. He has lost about half his blood volume: a PEA arrest from hemorrhage. The code team starts compressions and the surgeon is called to the bedside.

orRecovered.label: To the OR, by a slower route
orRecovered.narrative: He reaches the OR {(t - onset)|duration} after the bleeding started, but deeper in shock, with more crystalloid or later blood than an early call would have needed. The bleeding is controlled; the extra hours of shock raise the risk of kidney injury and coagulopathy.

expertPath.text: HR has crept up about 7 since handover and he is restless. Look at him and check the drains: the left drain is bright red, about 70 mL in 15 min.
Draw labs with a type and crossmatch. Page the surgeon with an SBAR naming bleeding and asking them to come now.
Callback: blood ordered. Request emergency-release units, activate the massive transfusion protocol, warm him, start a 500 mL crystalloid bridge only.
Emergency units at the bedside: transfuse both through the warmer. The first hemoglobin is close to baseline: it lags.
Surgeon at the bedside: back to the OR, about 15 min.
First cooler: red cells with plasma 1:1 and platelets; calcium chloride as the citrated units run in.
Leaves for the OR about 33 min after the bleeding started, MAP never below 60.

orTarget.headline: To the OR early, resuscitated with blood
orTarget.body: You saw the drift, found the bleeding, got the surgeon there and gave blood instead of more crystalloid. That is the expert path.

orRecovered.headline: To the OR, by a slower route
orRecovered.body: He made it, but later or deeper in shock than he needed to. Look at the minutes before the call, the first blood and how much crystalloid went in: the vital signs were drifting before the pressure fell.

arrest.headline: Cardiac arrest from blood loss
arrest.body: The bleeding outran the response. The most useful kind of run to learn from: find the point where the HR, pulse pressure and drain output first told the story, and what a call then would have changed.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: The run reached its time limit without a return to the OR.

scoring.modelReasoning: Early post-operative hemorrhage after a Whipple, from the operative bed, with compensated hemorrhagic shock. The clues: the heart rate creeping up, the pulse pressure narrowing while the systolic pressure still looks acceptable, the left drain turning bright red, a firmer abdomen, restlessness and cooler hands, then falling urine output and a rising lactate. The first hemoglobin is close to baseline because whole blood is being lost; it falls only as the vessels refill and fluid is given. The fix is surgical, so the surgeon comes now. Until then: blood early (emergency-release units, then the massive transfusion protocol with plasma and platelets), crystalloid only as a short bridge, warming, calcium as citrated units go in, and a pressure target agreed with the surgeon rather than a normal number chased with fluid or a vasopressor.

focusedStart.label: Start as the vital signs drift
focusedStart.summary: Join at 18:08, six minutes after the bleeding started: the heart rate has crept up a few beats and nothing has alarmed yet.

source.note: Tick 480 is 6 min after onset. With no learner action the first alarm (HR 110) comes at about 26 min and the written question at about 14 min, so the start is reached with nothing open and leaves recognition to the learner. The drains criterion is left out of a focused run, because the expert path checks the drains at 18:07 (recognizeExpertAt, tick 420).

hgbLags.ask: The first hemoglobin is about to come back. If it is close to his post-op 11.2, does that rule out bleeding?

choices.label: Yes: bleeding would have dropped it
No: the hemoglobin lags behind acute blood loss

hgbLags.explain: Whole blood is lost at the same hemoglobin concentration, so the number barely moves at first. It falls as fluid refills the vessels and as crystalloid is given. The trauma bleeding guideline recommends repeated hemoglobin measurements because a normal first value can mask early bleeding.

source.cite: Rossaint R, Afshari A, Bouillon B, et al. The European guideline on management of major bleeding and coagulopathy following trauma: sixth edition. Crit Care 2023;27:80. doi:10.1186/s13054-023-04327-7
source.note: FLAG: the guideline's point that a single normal hemoglobin can mask early bleeding is confirmed here from summaries (see the document sources), not the sixth edition's own text. The mechanism (whole-blood loss, then dilution) is the scenario's model.

bridge.ask: The emergency-release blood is about 10 minutes away. How much crystalloid until it arrives?

choices.label: As much as it takes to get the pressure back to normal
A short bridge only (about 1 L or less), then blood

bridge.explain: Crystalloid carries no oxygen and no clotting factors; most of it leaves the vessels within the hour and it dilutes and cools. ATLS (11th edition) asks for crystalloid only as a minimal bridge until blood is available.

source.cite: Advanced Trauma Life Support, 11th edition (American College of Surgeons, 2025), as summarized in: Advanced trauma life support 2025: a brief review of updates. Injury 2026;57(4):113079. doi:10.1016/j.injury.2026.113079
source.note: Read through a secondary summary (JournalFeed, 2026) on 2026-11-10, not the course manual: minimize crystalloid as a bridging fluid until blood is available, balanced 1:1:1 component therapy or low-titer O whole blood, early massive transfusion protocol activation, permissive hypotension until hemorrhage control. The summary gives no numeric hemorrhage BP target and does not reproduce the hemorrhage class table.

ratio.ask: The first cooler is coming. How should the red cells be given?

choices.label: Red cells alone until the coags come back

ratio.explain: Massive transfusion guidance gives plasma with red cells between 1:1 and 1:2, plus one apheresis platelet unit per six red cells, without waiting 45 minutes for coags. In PROPPR (trauma), 1:1:1 had more hemostasis and fewer deaths from exsanguination in 24 h than 1:1:2, with no difference in 24-h or 30-day mortality.

source.cite: American College of Surgeons TQIP, Massive Transfusion in Trauma Guidelines (October 2014); Holcomb JB, Tilley BC, Baraniuk S, et al. Transfusion of plasma, platelets, and red blood cells in a 1:1:1 vs a 1:1:2 ratio and mortality in patients with severe trauma: the PROPPR randomized clinical trial. JAMA 2015;313(5):471-482
source.note: TQIP 2014 ratios read 2026-11-10; PROPPR results from a summary read 2026-11-10. Both are trauma evidence applied to a surgical bleed.

target.ask: Trauma guidelines suggest a systolic of 80-90 mmHg until bleeding is controlled. Does that number carry straight over to him?

choices.label: Not directly: it comes from trauma; agree a target with the surgeon
No: aim for a systolic over 120

target.explain: The permissive target comes from trauma patients without brain injury, before surgical control. There is no equivalent trial for a bleed after abdominal surgery in an older adult, so the target is agreed with the surgeon (here a MAP of about 65). What does carry over is the direction: don't chase a normal pressure with crystalloid or a vasopressor while the bleeding goes on.

source.cite: Rossaint R, Afshari A, Bouillon B, et al. The European guideline on management of major bleeding and coagulopathy following trauma: sixth edition. Crit Care 2023;27:80. doi:10.1186/s13054-023-04327-7
source.note: FLAG: indirect evidence. The 80-90 mmHg systolic target is the trauma guideline's (confirmed from a summary of the fifth edition); no guideline was found that sets a pressure target for post-operative abdominal hemorrhage, which is why the prompt asks the learner to agree one with the surgeon.

calcium.ask: Citrated red cells and plasma are running in fast. What happens to his ionized calcium?
calcium.explain: Each unit carries citrate anticoagulant, which binds calcium. Low ionized calcium weakens clotting and the heart, so massive transfusion guidance checks it at baseline and at least hourly and replaces it.

source.cite: American College of Surgeons TQIP, Massive Transfusion in Trauma Guidelines (October 2014)
source.note: Monitoring and correction of hypocalcemia read 2026-11-10; the citrate mechanism is the scenario's model (FLAG: not quoted from the guideline).
